definition: The practice of tracking users across multiple websites to build detailed profiles of their browsing behavior, preferences, and interests for advertising and analytics purposes.
metaDescription: Learn about cross site tracking: how companies monitor your web browsing across multiple sites to build detailed user profiles for targeted advertising.
simpleExplanation: Cross site tracking is like having someone follow you around different stores in a mall, taking notes about what you look at and buy. Companies use various techniques to track your activity across different websites to learn about your interests.
whyItMatters: This tracking creates detailed profiles about your personal interests, habits, and behavior without your explicit consent. It can lead to privacy invasion, discriminatory pricing, and manipulation through highly targeted advertising.
technicalDetail: Cross site tracking uses methods like third-party cookies, web beacons, browser fingerprinting, and tracking pixels embedded across websites. Companies like Google and Facebook operate extensive tracking networks that can monitor users across millions of websites to build comprehensive behavioral profiles.

examples.explanation: Facebook Like buttons and Twitter share buttons on websites can track your visits even if you don't click them, building a profile of sites you browse.
Google's ad network places cookies on millions of websites, allowing them to see that the same person visited a shoe store, then a travel site, then a restaurant review page.
Google Analytics is used by millions of websites, giving Google insight into user behavior across a vast portion of the internet, even on sites that aren't Google properties.
